name: Kerma culture
info: The Kerma culture, or Kingdom of Kerma, was a Nubian kingdom on the Nile in present-day Sudan from about 2500 to 1500 BCE that grew to rival Egypt, raided deep into it and left a great mudbrick temple and royal tumuli.

facts.homeland: Upper Nubia, in present-day northern and central Sudan, centred on Kerma; at its height from the First to the Fourth Cataract; key sites Kerma with its Western Deffufa, Doukki Gel and Sai Island
facts.period: Pre-Kerma c. 3500–2500 BCE; Early Kerma c. 2500–2000 BCE; Middle Kerma c. 2000–1750 BCE; Classic Kerma c. 1750–1500 BCE; conquered by Egypt c. 1504 BCE, with rebellions until c. 1300 BCE
facts.known: the Western Deffufa, a monumental mudbrick temple; great royal tumuli with human sacrifices; cattle skulls buried with kings; an army of archers; trade in gold, ivory, ebony and incense; the raid into Egypt c. 1575–1550 BCE
facts.sources: excavations at Kerma by George Andrew Reisner (1920s) and Charles Bonnet; surveys along the Nile and before the Merowe Dam; Egyptian inscriptions and records; ceramic sequences; skeletal and dental studies; ancient DNA (2022)

t: Kerma grew from a fortified village into a city of about 25 hectares, the capital of a centralised Nubian kingdom that controlled the Nile from the First to the Fourth Cataract.
Rich in gold, cattle, ivory and ebony, it traded with Egypt and fought it, raiding deep into Egypt around 1575–1550 BCE in alliance with the Hyksos.
Thutmose I of Egypt destroyed Kerma around 1504 BCE, but rebellions went on for two centuries, and the later Kingdom of Kush honoured Kerma as part of its past.
dyk: Egyptian royal statues and monuments looted in Kerma’s raid on Egypt were carried back to Kerma, and the defeat is believed to have been erased later from Egypt’s official records; it is known from an inscription in the tomb of the governor Sobeknakht II at Nekheb.
ev: The pre-Kerma culture develops in Upper Nubia, with small kingdoms and settled farming
A new fortified village at Kerma begins the Early Kerma period
Egypt’s Middle Kingdom builds forts in Lower Nubia, while Kerma fortifies Sai as its border
The Classic Kerma period begins: the city grows to about 25 hectares and the Western Deffufa is built
Kerma, allied with the Hyksos, invades deep into Egypt
After the campaigns of Thutmose I, Egypt annexes Kerma
George Andrew Reisner excavates Kerma, taking it for an Egyptian outpost
Charles Bonnet’s Swiss team finds a cache of granite statues of the Twenty-fifth Dynasty pharaohs at Kerma

sections.origins:
The Kerma culture takes its name from Kerma, a town in northern Sudan in the part of ancient Nubia called Upper Nubia. It was preceded by the pre-Kerma culture, which developed between about 3500 and 2500 BCE and formed statelets and small kingdoms, probably larger than those of the A-Group culture in Lower Nubia. The earliest settlement at Kerma, lying under the later cemetery, was a village of wooden buildings, with storage pits, cattle pens, two small rectangular buildings and fifty round huts, ringed by a wooden palisade and earthen walls. Upper Nubia had contact with the Old Kingdom of Egypt, and its early regional rulers seem at first to have been loyal to the Egyptian kings.

Archaeologists divide the Kerma culture by its pottery and other finds into periods that roughly match Egypt’s: Early Kerma (2500–2000 BCE), Middle Kerma (2000–1750 BCE) and Classic Kerma (1750–1500 BCE), followed by a Late or Post-Kerma phase under Egyptian rule. Over these centuries Kerma grew from a newly founded fortified village to a fortified town of 3 hectares and then a fully urban settlement of about 25 hectares.

Its people were mixed. Christian Simon’s study of the skeletons, as reported by Claude Rilly, found three main groups, one of which may descend from the pre-Kerma population that founded the new town 4 kilometres from the old settlement when the Nile’s bed shrank. A 2022 study of DNA from the hair of a farming and herding person at Kadruka, from about 2000 BCE, found them genetically indistinguishable from early pastoralists of Kenya and Tanzania, consistent with herders spreading south along the Nile.
sections.society:
Kerma was a sizeable kingdom: Egyptian records speak of its rich, populous farmland. Unlike Egypt, it seems to have been highly centralised, and at its height it controlled the Nile from the First to the Fourth Cataract, a domain as long as that of ancient Egypt. Most of its people lived in villages beside their fields, while some districts specialised in herding goats, sheep and cattle, or in processing gold. Certain towns gathered farm produce and directed trade. Surveys have found many Kerma sites south of the capital along now-dry channels of the Nile, and work ahead of the Merowe Dam traced them upriver at least as far as the Abu Hamad and Mograt Island area.

Only Kerma itself, with Doukki Gel, and Sai Island seem to have had large urban populations. Both show wealthy elites and a class of officials who watched over goods arriving from distant lands and supervised shipments from administrative buildings. Farming in the region dates back to the pre-Kerma period, and copper working is attested at Kerma from about 2200–2000 BCE.

Cattle mattered greatly. The royal tombs held the skulls of thousands of cattle, some brought from far districts, presumably as tribute from rural communities when a king died, which parallels the later importance of cattle as royal property elsewhere in Africa. Kerma’s army was built around archers. In the Classic period the kings were buried under great tumuli in the city’s cemetery, with many human sacrifices and secondary burials; two of the largest mounds were decorated with white quartzite cones.
sections.beliefs:
The religion of Kerma was quite different from the later Napatan and Meroitic traditions, which were shaped by the Egyptian gods brought to Upper Nubia under the New Kingdom. In the Classic Kerma period animals were shown in their full natural form, without the human bodies of Egyptian gods. Four animals held the highest importance: the ram, the lion, the winged hippopotamus and the winged giraffe. Amulets were common, and some seem to show mythical creatures.

Some scholars believe the people of Kerma held an animist view of the world, pointing to their treatment of Jebel Barkal as a sacred place, a tradition later taken up by the Egyptians of the New Kingdom, who built a great temple of Amun there. The later Nubian lion god Apedamak is thought to have grown out of Kerma’s reverence for lions, which were given human form as gods only in the Meroitic period.

At the centre of the city stood the Western Deffufa, a large monumental temple of mudbrick built in the Classic period.
sections.arts:
The periods of Kerma are defined largely by its pottery, which archaeologists use to date sites and trace the culture’s spread. Its builders worked in timber and earth at first, and later in fired mudbrick: during the Middle and Classic periods Egyptian influence shows in straight-walled mudbrick buildings, more elaborate burials and imported prestige goods. The Western Deffufa, a massive mudbrick temple, and the great royal tumuli are its largest monuments.

Copper metallurgy is attested at Kerma from about 2200–2000 BCE, and gold was processed in parts of the kingdom. The animal imagery of the Classic period, rams, lions and winged hippopotami and giraffes, appears in its art and on amulets.

The language of Kerma is unknown. Peter Behrens and Marianne Bechaus-Gerst argued from herding words borrowed into the Nubian language Nobiin that Kerma’s people spoke a Cushitic, Afroasiatic language. Claude Rilly instead proposes an Eastern Sudanic language of the Nilo-Saharan family, possibly ancestral to Meroitic. Julien Cooper, studying place names and personal names in Egyptian texts, finds that names from Kush look Eastern Sudanic while those from Lower Nubia look Afroasiatic, and suggests an Eastern Sudanic language was spoken at Kerma by at least 1800 BCE.
sections.exchange:
Kerma stood between Egypt and the African interior and played an important role in passing luxury goods from Central Africa to Egypt. Egypt coveted its gold, cattle, milk products, ebony, incense and ivory. The Gash Group of eastern Sudan and Eritrea was in contact with Kerma throughout its history, and its main site, Mahal Teglinos, became an important trading partner. By 2300 BCE the C-Group culture appeared in Lower Nubia, probably from the Dongola Reach near Kerma. As Egypt’s Old Kingdom collapsed, Kerma expanded north to Aswan.

Under the Middle Kingdom, Egypt campaigned in Lower Nubia, possibly to check Kerma, and Senusret I built forts at Ikkur, Quban, Aniba, Buhen and Kor to guard the border and the gold mines of Wadi Allaqi. Kerma strongly fortified Sai, its border with Lower Nubia. When Egyptian power weakened in the Second Intermediate Period, Kerma reached its height, absorbed the kingdom of Sai and allied with the Hyksos. An inscription in the tomb of Sobeknakht II at Nekheb records that Kerma invaded deep into Egypt between about 1575 and 1550 BCE.

The New Kingdom struck back. Thutmose I led several campaigns south that destroyed Kerma and ended in Egypt’s annexation of Nubia around 1504 BCE, with a frontier at Kanisah Kurgus beyond the Fourth Cataract. Rebellions continued for about 220 years, until around 1300 BCE.
sections.legacy:
Under Egyptian rule Kerma’s culture became increasingly Egyptian. Nubia was governed by a Viceroy of Kush, the “King’s Son of Kush”, Egyptian towns were founded on Sai Island and at Sedeinga, Soleb, Mirgissa and Sesibi, and major ceremonies were held at Jebel Barkal near Napata. Around 1000 BCE, about five centuries after Kerma’s fall, the more Egyptianised Kingdom of Kush emerged. How much it continued Kerma is hard to judge, but the early Kushite kings used Kerma for royal burials and ceremonies, their funerary compounds at Napata follow a similar plan, and caches of their statues were left at Kerma, suggesting that they saw a link with the old capital.

When George Andrew Reisner excavated Kerma in the 1920s, he took it for the base of an Egyptian governor whose successors became independent kings, because he found inscribed Egyptian statues in the great burials. From the mid-20th century excavations showed that the city was far larger and more complex, and that its material culture and burials were overwhelmingly local. The Swiss archaeologist Charles Bonnet was among the first to challenge Reisner, and it took twenty years for Egyptologists to accept his arguments.

In 2003 Bonnet’s team found near Kerma a cache of monumental black granite statues of the pharaohs of the Twenty-fifth Dynasty, among them Taharqa and Tanutamun, now shown in the Kerma Museum.

summary: The Kerma culture was the civilisation of a Nubian kingdom centred on Kerma in present-day Sudan from about 2500 to 1500 BCE. It grew into a centralised state controlling the Nile from the First to the Fourth Cataract, traded gold, ivory and cattle with Egypt and fought it. Egypt conquered it around 1504 BCE, and the later Kingdom of Kush kept a link with its old capital.

The article's 'History of archaeological research' section contains a stray, unsourced editorial sentence calling craniometry 'junk science' inside a quotation, and a garbled line on hair DNA; I left out the craniometric and cranial comparisons entirely and used only Christian Simon's three clusters (via Rilly) and the 2022 ancient-DNA study (Wang et al.).
The lede's 'ethnic melting pot' with roots in the Sahara, Central Africa and the Levant is not sourced in the body beyond the genetics; I wrote only 'Its people were mixed' with the specific studies.

The article spells the pharaoh 'Senwosret I' and 'Tanoutamon'; I used the usual English forms Senusret I and Tanutamun. Reference titles: the article misspells 'Pharaohs' and 'Archaéologie'; corrected in the reference list.
